desc:
You are given an integer array nums and an integer k. In one move you choose any element and overwrite it with any integer you like. You may make at most k moves.

The range of an array is its largest value minus its smallest value. Return the smallest range you can obtain.

nums = [5, 3, 2, 4], k = 2             -> 1
nums = [1, 5, 0, 10, 14], k = 3        -> 1
nums = [6, 6, 0, 1, 1, 4, 4, 0], k = 2 -> 4

In the first example keep 3 and 4 and overwrite 5 and 2 with 3 and 4: the array becomes [3, 3, 4, 4] with range 1.
hints: Elements you overwrite can be given any value, so they never hurt the range if you pick a value inside it. Only the elements you keep determine the range.
You keep at least n - k elements (and at least one). To make their range small, which elements should you keep: ones that are close together in value.
Sort the array. The kept elements can be taken as a window of consecutive values in sorted order, of size n - k. Slide that window and take the smallest last - first. If k ≥ n - 1 the answer is 0.
editorial: Overwritten elements can be set to a value equal to one of the kept elements, so they do not widen the range. The problem becomes: choose which m = n - k elements to keep (all k moves should be used when they help) so that their max minus min is smallest. If m ≤ 1, one kept element (or none) gives range 0.

After sorting, any set of m kept elements has range at least that of the m consecutive sorted elements starting at its minimum, because replacing the kept set by the m consecutive elements from its smallest member never increases the maximum. So we only look at windows of m consecutive sorted values and return the minimum a[i + m - 1] - a[i].
Sorting is O(n log n) and the window sweep is O(n). The largest answer is 2*10<sup>9</sup>, which still fits in a signed 32-bit integer.
